subject_line: Jack Shine's shoebox of letters in The Paper Man
email_body:
Dear Billy,

In The Paper Man, Jack Shine finds a shoebox of letters among his mother's things in 1980s Cork and is pulled into the life of Matthias Sindelar. Linking a Cork household to an Austrian footballer is an unusual bridge.

How did you first come across the Sindelar story, and why tell it through letters found decades later?

subject_line: Jamie's currach in How to Build a Boat

Why a currach, of all things, as what brings these characters together? And did your teaching shape the school scenes?

subject_line: Memory and forgetting in Tell Me What I Am
email_body:
Dear Una,

Tell Me What I Am follows Nessa searching for her sister Deena while Ruby grows up on Lake Champlain. You've described it as, beyond the crime elements, a book about how we remember and how we forget.

I'd like to explore how you decided what Ruby would be allowed to remember, and how writing from Sligo shaped a story set in America.

After two Mayo story collections, what changed for you in sustaining the town across a full novel?

Do you think of your work as political while writing it, and has teaching at the University of Limerick changed how you think about voice?

subject_line: Eithne's tower in The Poison Glen
email_body:
Dear Annemarie,

The Poison Glen returns to Balor locking his daughter Eithne in a tower on Tory Island, voicing Eithne, her handmaids and her mother against the history of Ireland's mother and baby homes.

How did the Balor story present itself as a way into that history, and how did the handmaids' voices come to you?

email_body:
Dear Rose,

I keep coming back to the story in Oddbody where a waitress gives birth to an egg in the middle of her breakfast shift. Such an ordinary setting for something so strange.

I'd love to ask you how you decide where the line sits between the everyday and the uncanny in a story, and whether Waterford shaped that sense of things being slightly wrong.

subject_line: Doctor Troy, Ronnie and the baby in Faha
email_body:
Dear Niall,

Time of the Child stayed with me for the way a single event, a baby left in the care of Doctor Jack Troy and his daughter Ronnie in December 1962, reorders a whole parish. You've said Kiltumper is not Faha, which is an amalgamation of estuary villages.

I'd love to ask how you build a place like that from pieces of real ones, and what returning to Faha after This Is Happiness asked of you.

subject_line: The two sequences that open Giving Birth to My Father
email_body:
Dear Tusiata,

In Giving Birth to My Father I was struck by the opening pair of sequences, one imagining how your father's death was supposed to go and the other recording how it actually went, after his return to Sāmoa from fifty years in Aotearoa. The title's sense that a death in Sāmoan culture is also a birth carries the whole book.

I'd love to ask why you chose to set the imagined version beside the real one.

subject_line: From embroidered panels to Standing on my Shadow
email_body:

I'd love to ask whether the new collection has a hidden map of its own shaped by caring for the va.

subject_line: Kotaz, Ndiyoyika and writing in two languages
email_body:

I'd love to ask what changed for you when you wrote a whole collection in isiXhosa after three in English, and how editing Kotaz has shaped your sense of which language a poem belongs in.

book_title: Sankomota: An Ode in One Album – A Reflective Essay
subject_line: Writing a whole essay around one Sankomota album
email_body:
Dear Phehello,

I came across Sankomota: An Ode in One Album, your reflective essay built around a single record,, an unusual form: a book-length act of listening. It sits alongside your work editing BKO Poetry & Literature Magazine and the conversations you have hosted with writers such as Sabata-mpho Mokae.

I'd love to ask why that particular album demanded an essay, and how your training in drama and film shaped the way you wrote about music.
